title: Trump Testifies His Net Worth Fluctuated With Markets and Feelings
description_medium: In a 2007 deposition in his defamation suit against journalist Timothy O’Brien, Donald Trump was asked how he calculated his net worth. Trump said the figure moved with markets and with attitudes and feelings, including his own. O’Brien’s 2005 book had placed Trump’s wealth far below his public claims. A New Jersey appellate court later affirmed dismissal of Trump’s suit, finding the challenged statements were not shown to be made with actual malice.
description_long: Donald Trump gave the deposition while suing Timothy O’Brien over statements in O’Brien’s 2005 book, TrumpNation, which estimated Trump’s net worth at $150 million to $250 million, far below Trump’s own public figures. Asked whether his net worth went up and down with markets and with his feelings, Trump agreed and described the estimate as changing with markets, attitudes and feelings, including his own. The testimony illustrates that his public net-worth figure was not a single fixed calculation. It should not be described as an admission that he lied: the deposition concerned Trump’s defamation claim, and the New Jersey appellate court affirmed dismissal in 2011 because the record did not establish actual malice by O’Brien. The testimony is relevant to how Trump described his valuation, while the litigation outcome addressed whether O’Brien’s statements could support a defamation judgment. This record does not establish that the deposition itself proved a later fraud claim.
evidence_notes: CBS reports Trump’s deposition answer and O’Brien’s book estimate. The New Jersey Appellate Division opinion confirms the defamation litigation and 2011 dismissal; it does not establish that Trump admitted lying.
corrected_wording: Proposed correction: Trump Testifies His Net Worth Fluctuated With Markets and Feelings. Correct factual overclaims and chronology as described in evidence_notes.

title: Trump Speaks at CPAC as He Considers a 2016 Run
description_medium: Donald Trump addressed the Conservative Political Action Conference in National Harbor, Maryland, on March 6, 2014, at a time when he was publicly discussing another presidential campaign. A transcript records remarks on trade and China alongside his political comments. The appearance documents Trump’s participation in conservative movement politics, but the available sources do not establish that it marked the start of organized campaign preparations or that he placed second in CPAC’s 2014 straw poll.
description_long: Trump’s March 6, 2014, appearance at the Conservative Political Action Conference took place while he was considering another presidential run. The event transcript records an address to the conference audience and includes his criticism of U.S. trade relations with China, a recurring theme in his public remarks. Trump had floated presidential ambitions before, including during the 1990s, so the speech belongs in a longer record of political positioning rather than proving that a formal 2016 campaign began that day. The source material supports the date, venue and substance of the public appearance; it does not identify a donor operation, consulting team or systematic message-testing effort launched at CPAC. Nor should the account claim a second-place straw-poll finish: the 2014 straw-poll winner was Rand Paul, and the supplied material does not substantiate Trump’s placing. The documented event is a conference speech and expression of political interest, not an established campaign launch.
evidence_notes: The transcript supports the CPAC speech and date. WaPo reported Rand Paul won the straw poll, correcting the unsupported second-place claim; campaign organization claims are not sourced.
corrected_wording: Proposed correction: Trump Speaks at CPAC as He Considers a 2016 Run. Correct factual overclaims and chronology as described in evidence_notes.

title: Trump Wins 2024 Election
description_medium: Donald Trump defeated Vice President Kamala Harris in the November 5, 2024, presidential election, returning to the White House after his 2020 defeat. The National Archives records 312 electoral votes for Trump and 226 for Harris; Trump also won the national popular vote. Those results establish the election outcome, but do not by themselves show that voters endorsed every policy or promise associated with either campaign.
description_long: The November 5, 2024, election returned Donald Trump to the presidency after he defeated Vice President Kamala Harris. The official Electoral College count gave Trump 312 votes and Harris 226, and Trump also received more votes nationwide. The result completed a political comeback: Trump had lost the 2020 election to Joe Biden, left office in January 2021, and then won the Republican nomination again in 2024. The outcome made him the first former president since Grover Cleveland to win a nonconsecutive second term. Electoral and popular-vote totals describe who won; they do not establish voter agreement with every position, proposal or future action of the winning candidate. For that reason, the result should not be presented as proof of a mandate for a particular agenda or a campaign of retribution. This entry records the certified election outcome and return to office, while interpretations of voter motivation require separate polling or other evidence.
evidence_notes: National Archives confirms 312–226 Electoral College result; popular-vote victory reported contemporaneously. Removed unsupported inference that the result constituted a mandate for particular policies.
corrected_wording: Proposed correction: Trump Wins 2024 Election. Correct factual overclaims and chronology as described in evidence_notes.

title: Gaetz Withdraws, Trump Nominates Pam Bondi
description_medium: On November 21, 2024, Matt Gaetz withdrew from consideration as Donald Trump’s nominee for attorney general after his selection drew scrutiny and opposition in Congress. Trump announced former Florida attorney general Pam Bondi as his replacement that evening. The change ended Gaetz’s nomination before a confirmation hearing and shifted the transition’s focus to Bondi. Claims about Gaetz’s alleged misconduct and Bondi’s earlier role in a Florida investigation are separate matters and are not established by this nomination sequence.
description_long: Trump selected Gaetz, then a Florida Republican congressman, to lead the Justice Department during the transition after the 2024 election. The choice prompted scrutiny over a House Ethics Committee investigation and allegations of sexual misconduct, which Gaetz denied. On November 21, Gaetz announced he was withdrawing, saying he did not want his nomination to become a distraction. Trump then named Pam Bondi, Florida’s former attorney general, as his new choice for the post. The sequence is significant as a rapid change in the incoming administration’s attorney-general selection before Senate consideration began. Bondi later went through the confirmation process separately. The withdrawal and replacement do not resolve the allegations concerning Gaetz, nor do they substantiate claims that Bondi had acted improperly in a distinct Florida matter involving Trump University. Those claims require their own evidence and should not be implied as the reason for her selection. This account is limited to the nomination change and the stated context for Gaetz’s departure.
evidence_notes: Reuters supports the withdrawal and Bondi selection. Avoids converting allegations or a separate Trump University donation controversy into a causal claim about the nomination.
corrected_wording: Proposed correction: Gaetz Withdraws, Trump Nominates Pam Bondi. Correct factual overclaims and chronology as described in evidence_notes.

title: Trump Promises Clemency for January 6 Defendants Before Inauguration
description_medium: Before taking office in January 2025, Donald Trump repeatedly promised clemency for people charged or convicted over the January 6, 2021, Capitol attack. In a December interview, he said he would consider pardons on his first day, though the proposed scope varied in his public comments. The promise preceded the clemency actions he issued after inauguration, which included pardons and commutations. His characterization of defendants as “hostages” was rhetoric, not a description of their legal status.
description_long: During the 2024 campaign and transition, Trump said he would grant clemency to at least some people prosecuted over the January 6 attack on the U.S. Capitol. His statements varied in scope: at different times he discussed pardoning all, most, or selected defendants, and in a December 2024 interview he said he would look at the matter immediately. The distinction between promise and action matters. On January 20, 2025, after returning to office, Trump issued an order granting full pardons to many January 6 defendants and commuting the sentences of others; the order also directed dismissal of pending cases. At his inauguration-day events, he used the word “hostages” for people prosecuted in connection with the attack, although they had been defendants or prisoners under the criminal justice system. These steps represented a sweeping use of presidential clemency, but the earlier pledge alone did not specify every recipient or outcome. The entry focuses on the pre-inauguration commitment and separates it from the later order that carried it out.
evidence_notes: AP documents the varying pre-inauguration pledge and Jan. 20 clemency action. Presidency Project transcript records the “hostages” phrasing. Keep pledge and subsequent order distinct.
corrected_wording: Proposed correction: Trump Promises Clemency for January 6 Defendants Before Inauguration. Correct factual overclaims and chronology as described in evidence_notes.

title: Trump Seeks to End Birthright Citizenship by Executive Order
description_medium: On January 20, 2025, President Donald Trump signed an executive order directing federal agencies not to recognize citizenship for some children born in the United States based on their parents’ immigration status. The order challenged the longstanding interpretation of the Fourteenth Amendment’s Citizenship Clause and prompted immediate lawsuits. Courts blocked its implementation. The directive therefore attempted to change federal practice but did not itself end birthright citizenship; litigation over its legality continued after the initial injunctions.
description_long: Trump signed the order on his first day back in office, directing federal agencies to withhold recognition of U.S. citizenship from children born in the country if their mother was unlawfully present or only temporarily present and their father was neither a U.S. citizen nor a lawful permanent resident. The administration argued that the Citizenship Clause did not cover those circumstances. The order drew swift legal challenges from states and affected individuals, who argued that the Fourteenth Amendment’s guarantee of citizenship to people born in the United States applied regardless of their parents’ status. Federal judges issued injunctions preventing the policy from taking effect. In June 2025, the Supreme Court limited the scope of certain nationwide injunctions in Trump v. CASA, but that procedural ruling did not decide whether the citizenship order was constitutional; a certified class injunction also remained in place. Thus the January directive did not end birthright citizenship. It initiated a major constitutional dispute about the scope of the Citizenship Clause and the reach of federal courts’ remedies. The entry describes the executive action and challenge without claiming a final merits ruling.
evidence_notes: White House EO text supports its scope. SCOTUSblog summarizes June 2025 partial stay of universal injunctions; this was not a decision on constitutionality. Description distinguishes policy from outcome.
corrected_wording: Proposed correction: Trump Seeks to End Birthright Citizenship by Executive Order. Correct factual overclaims and chronology as described in evidence_notes.

title: Trump Removes Joint Chiefs Chairman Charles Q. Brown
description_medium: On February 21, 2025, President Donald Trump removed Air Force Gen. Charles Q. Brown Jr. as chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff and nominated retired Air Force Lt. Gen. Dan Caine to replace him. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth separately announced planned leadership changes affecting the Navy and Air Force. These moves occurred about a month after Trump’s inauguration, not on Inauguration Day. The report documents the personnel decisions but does not establish retaliation or a plan to secure military obedience.
description_long: Brown had served as chairman of the Joint Chiefs since 2023, after President Joe Biden nominated him to the role. Trump announced his removal on February 21, 2025, and nominated Caine, a retired Air Force officer, to succeed him. The chairman is the highest-ranking military officer and principal military adviser to the president and defense secretary, but does not exercise operational command over U.S. forces. On the same day, Hegseth said the administration planned to replace Navy chief Lisa Franchetti and Air Force vice chief James Slife. Those were additional leadership changes, not all completed dismissals of Joint Chiefs members at that moment. The timing and scope differ from the entry’s original claim of several firings on January 20. The contemporaneous report establishes the chairman’s removal and the announced plans; it does not demonstrate that the decision was retaliation for past disagreement or designed to facilitate domestic military deployments. The record is therefore about a February leadership change and its named personnel, not a day-one purge or an established motive.
evidence_notes: NPR supports Brown’s February 21 removal, Caine nomination, and announced plans concerning Franchetti and Slife. Motive claims are omitted; date correction is proposed.
corrected_wording: Proposed correction: Trump Removes Joint Chiefs Chairman Charles Q. Brown. Correct factual overclaims and chronology as described in evidence_notes.

title: Trump Orders Federal Agencies to Define Sex as Male or Female
description_medium: On January 20, 2025, Donald Trump signed Executive Order 14168, directing federal agencies to use definitions of sex as male or female in official policy, documents and communications. The order also directed agencies to remove references to “gender” in specified federal materials and told the State Department to issue passports reflecting sex as defined by the order. It was a federal policy directive; it was separate from later orders on military service and women’s sports. Its provisions faced legal challenges and did not themselves abolish every form of transgender recognition or protection.
description_long: Executive Order 14168, signed on January 20, 2025, instructed federal agencies to define sex in terms of male or female and to apply those definitions when interpreting federal statutes, regulations and guidance. It directed agencies to remove references to gender identity from federal policies and documents in specified contexts. The order also instructed the State Department to ensure that government-issued identification documents, including passports, accurately reflect sex as defined in the order. These provisions affected federal administration and documentation, while their scope and implementation were subject to legal and operational constraints. The January order should not be conflated with the separate February executive order concerning participation in women’s sports or a distinct policy on military service. Nor does the order alone support a claim that transgender people lost all federal protections overnight. This entry records the signed directive and its stated agency-wide definitions; evaluating particular effects requires examining the relevant agency actions and court rulings. The administration described the change as restoring biological definitions, while civil-rights advocates challenged its impact on transgender people.
evidence_notes: White House EO text describes the definitions and agency instructions. Sports order is separately dated and expressly incorporates EO 14168’s definitions; avoid merging unrelated military or detention policies.
corrected_wording: Proposed correction: Trump Orders Federal Agencies to Define Sex as Male or Female. Correct factual overclaims and chronology as described in evidence_notes.

title: Trump Administration Moves to Fire Probationary Federal Workers
description_medium: In February 2025, the Trump administration directed agencies to identify and dismiss many probationary federal employees as part of its effort to reduce the federal workforce. Probationary employees, often in their first year of service, generally have fewer procedural protections than permanent staff. Thousands received termination notices across agencies, though a notice did not necessarily mean a separation was completed. The drive came after Trump took office and was not a transition-team action before inauguration. Federal unions and employees challenged aspects of the process in court.
description_long: The administration’s workforce reductions escalated in February 2025, when the Office of Personnel Management instructed agencies to review probationary employees and the White House pressed for broad cuts. Probationary workers are generally new hires or employees in a new position who have not completed a trial period; they can have fewer appeal rights than career civil servants, but agencies still must follow applicable laws and procedures. Thousands of employees received termination notices, including workers at the Forest Service and other departments. Reporting described confusion over notices, reversals and whether agencies had completed the dismissals. The administration said it was removing employees it considered noncritical and reducing federal spending. Unions and nonprofit groups challenged the mass-firing approach, arguing that the government had bypassed required procedures. A federal judge temporarily blocked some directives in February, while the litigation did not amount to a blanket finding about every individual termination. The reported effort began after Trump’s inauguration, so it should not be attributed to his transition team or described as advance implementation of Schedule F without evidence. Notices, completed separations and later court orders are distinct stages of the episode.
evidence_notes: Guardian reporting supports February agency directives, notices, affected probationary workforce and subsequent temporary court order. Corrected chronology; distinguish notices from completed separations.
corrected_wording: Proposed correction: Trump Administration Moves to Fire Probationary Federal Workers. Correct factual overclaims and chronology as described in evidence_notes.

title: Hegseth Confirmed as Defense Secretary After Contested Hearings
description_medium: The Senate confirmed Pete Hegseth as secretary of defense on January 24, 2025, by a 51–50 vote, with Vice President JD Vance casting the tie-breaker. Hegseth, a former Fox News host and Army National Guard officer, faced questions during his confirmation process about allegations of sexual misconduct, alcohol use and financial management at a veterans organization he had led. He denied wrongdoing. Three Republican senators joined Democrats in opposing him, leaving the chamber evenly divided before Vance’s vote.
description_long: Trump nominated Pete Hegseth, a former Fox News host and Army National Guard officer, to lead the Defense Department during the presidential transition. His confirmation hearings and subsequent debate focused on his management of veterans’ organizations and allegations concerning sexual conduct and alcohol use; Hegseth denied wrongdoing. On January 24, 2025, the Senate voted 50–50 on confirmation, with three Republican senators joining Democrats in opposition. Vice President JD Vance then cast the tie-breaking vote, producing a final 51–50 confirmation. The close outcome was unusual for a defense secretary nomination and reflected concerns raised by senators about Hegseth’s qualifications and personal conduct. The vote installed him as the civilian head of the department responsible for U.S. military policy and oversight. This account distinguishes allegations and questions raised during confirmation from established findings. Hegseth had military service in the Army National Guard, so characterizing him as having no military experience is inaccurate; the debate instead concerned the suitability of his record and leadership for the cabinet post. His later policy actions are separate events and are not included here.
evidence_notes: CBS and Roll Call support January 24 date, 50–50 before Vance’s tiebreak and final 51–50 confirmation. Sources identify Hegseth as an Army National Guard officer. Allegations are attributed and described as allegations.
corrected_wording: Proposed correction: Hegseth Confirmed as Defense Secretary After Contested Hearings. Correct factual overclaims and chronology as described in evidence_notes.
